source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) sycophancy in Wason 2-4-6 with GPT-5.1
finding: The AI chose the test sequences, not the human. A random-sequence generator gave the best human discovery rate. A generator told to disconfirm the user's hypothesis helped less than random. Gap 6 answer: the 29.5% rate is restored only by hypothesis-independent sampling, not by disconfirmation.
numbers: 557 recruited, 504 in discovery analyses. Discovery: random 29.5%, disconfirming 14.1%, agreeable 11.8%, confirming 8.4%, default GPT 5.9%. Chi-square(4)=28.02, p<.001. Default vs disconfirming 8.2 points, p=.043 one-sided only. Confidence change round 3 minus round 1: confirming +9.5, default +5.4, disconfirming -20.6, random -56.8; F(4,507)=72.67, eta2=.36.
limits: Rule was 'all numbers even'. Abstract low-stakes task. Hypotheses coded by Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, not the preregistered coder. Does not report positive vs negative test shares. Not a test of agents that choose their own tests.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a 'disconfirm the user's idea' prompt alone. A test generator that ignores the seeded hypothesis (broad, hypothesis-independent probes) did best. Seed hypotheses should not steer which tests the agent runs.

source: Chari and Pattanaik (2026) Wild Guesses and Mild Guesses in Active Concept Learning
finding: In an LLM-proposal Bayesian learner on the Number Game, expected-information-gain (EIG) queries are not better than positive-test queries on easy rules, but win when falsification is needed (compound rules). All methods fail when the generator gives the target almost no mass. Answers gap 4: policy winner depends on concept complexity.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Flash as proposer, max 50 queries, convergence at 0.95 posterior. Easy rules: EIG 3-8 queries vs PTS 2-6 vs passive 2-5. Medium: e.g. one rule EIG 8, PTS did not finish, passive 13; another EIG 17, PTS 31, passive 17. Hard: 'digits sum to <8' EIG 43, PTS and passive did not finish; several hard rules did not finish for all.
quote: EIG tends to select boundary points that maximize predictive entropy
limits: Workshop submission under review. Table text extraction is garbled, so rule-to-number alignment is uncertain for some rows. Single proposer model. Number Game only, no business task.
agent_relevance: Use a switch: cheap positive tests first, then discriminating or falsifying tests when progress stalls or contradictions appear. Authors state this meta-policy but did not test it.

source: Branchini, Bianchi and Burro (2025) Thinking in opposites improves hypothesis testing in Wason's rule-discovery task
finding: Original human result behind Think-in-Opposites. Training to think of opposites raised success from about 37% to 78%. Training to list properties did nothing. Benefit was at the first attempt.
numbers: N=180, 60 per condition. Success: opposites 78.33%, properties 38.33%, control 36.66%. Omnibus chi-square(2)=27.986, p<.001. More descending triples tested in opposites group, chi-square(2)=35.986.
limits: Psychology students, one task only; authors say generalising to hypothesis testing in general is not tenable. No effect sizes reported. Solution time longer in both training groups. No LLM test in this paper.
agent_relevance: The human effect is large but task-specific. It shows the prompt targets one concrete behavior (testing triples that break the current rule), not a general 'be critical' attitude.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, Think-in-Opposites table
finding: Gap 2 partial answer. Think-in-Opposites raised success for every model on the Wason task, but gains are significant for thinking models and mixed for non-thinking ones. Transfer beyond rule games is only via distillation, not a direct business test.
numbers: Success baseline to TiO: Qwen3-8B thinking 0.21 to 0.36, non-thinking 0.06 to 0.06; Qwen3-14B thinking 0.34 to 0.48, non-thinking 0.23 to 0.29; Qwen3-32B thinking 0.41 to 0.61, non-thinking 0.33 to 0.36; Llama-3.3-70B 0.21 to 0.38; GPT-4o 0.11 to 0.16; QwQ-32B 0.50 to 0.59; Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.73 to 0.78. 80 test episodes, 45-turn cap. Qwen3-32B thinking I:C 0.14 to 0.54.
limits: Synthetic rule sets only. Authors say real-world scientific discovery, QA and agentic tasks remain untested. Distilled-model transfer: GSM8K loss at most about 2%, AIME 2025 gains in earlier lines (a19, b14).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for open business or forecasting questions. For non-thinking models do not expect the prompt alone to help; for thinking models it is cheap and effective on rule tasks.

source: Failing to Falsify token cost per turn (same paper, Table 2)
finding: Gap 9 partial answer. The Think-in-Opposites prompt adds roughly 40% more tokens per turn for one thinking model, while lifting success 0.41 to 0.61. No best-of-N comparison at equal tokens was reported.
numbers: Qwen3-32B thinking: about 1,030 tokens per turn at baseline, about 1,450 with TiO (+about 41%). Success 0.41 to 0.61 (+20 points). Monetary cost not reported.
limits: The per-turn figure is from the page extraction summary of Table 2, one model only. No equal-token best-of-N arm found in any opened source.
agent_relevance: A test-first prompt costs tokens per turn but is cheaper than sampling many full runs; the equal-token comparison still has to be run by us.

source: Huang et al. (2025) Popper: automated hypothesis validation with agentic sequential falsifications
finding: An agent that designs falsification experiments for a hypothesis, with sequential testing to control Type-I error, matched human scientists on hypothesis validation and was faster. Closest measured system to an 'assumption test' step; domain is data analysis, not business.
numbers: Nominal alpha 0.1. Popper Type-I error 0.103 / 0.082 / 0.085 (DiscoveryBench / TargetVal-IL2 / IFNG), power 0.638 / 0.580 / 0.591. ReAct power 0.383 / 0.010 / 0.020; Self-Refine 0.476 / 0.183 / 0.067. Fisher combined test power 0.741 / 0.800 / 0.650 but Type-I error 0.311 / 0.264 / 0.173. DiscoveryBench 86 non-null hypotheses, 3 tests max; TargetVal 5 tests max.
limits: Statistical hypotheses over tables, not strategic assumptions. LLM cost and tokens not found in the part read. Baselines uncontrolled for tokens.
agent_relevance: Shows that a structured loop (propose test, run, combine evidence with error control) beats free-form agent loops and self-refinement. Supports S7 as a tool-backed test, not a reflection.

source: Huang et al. (2025) Popper human study and error analysis
finding: Against 9 human participants Popper was about 10 times faster. Its most common failures were reading p-values wrongly and picking tests that do not break the implication.
numbers: 11 recruited, 9 completed, 18 tasks. Popper 9.7x faster, 3.6x more code lines, 2.5x more statistical tests. Agent-human rating agreement Spearman 0.55 (p=5e-6); human Kendall W=0.91 over 90 proposals. Of 128 failed logs: misread p-values 35.9%, ineffective test selection 28.1%, tests breaking implication 17.2%, wrong implementation 8.6%, missing data 7.0%.
limits: Small human sample, one task type.
agent_relevance: Test design failures (28.1% + 17.2% = 45.3% of failed logs) are the main risk: add a check that a test's outcome would actually change the decision.

source: Si et al. (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Gap 7 proxy. LLM research ideas that reviewers rated above human ideas lost more score once executed. Pre-execution judgment is a poor stand-in for tested outcomes. Not a founder study.
numbers: 43 executors (19 human ideas, 24 AI ideas), 58 reviewers, 181 reviews. Ideation to execution: AI overall 5.382 to 3.406 (gap -1.976), human 4.596 to 3.968 (gap -0.628). Gap difference human minus AI: novelty 1.039 (p=.025), excitement 1.835 (p=.001), effectiveness 1.827 (p=.003), overall 1.348 (p=.004). After execution AI below human on all four means but not significant at idea level (N=43). Ideation-execution correlation for AI excitement -0.321.
limits: Research ideas in NLP, not startups. Small N. Between-group execution gaps significant; final-score ranking not significant.
agent_relevance: Evidence that plans and ideas that look good before testing can fail when run. Supports putting a real test before commitment and distrusting LLM self-ratings.

source: Csaszar, Ketkar and Kim (2024) AI and Strategic Decision-Making: entrepreneurs and investors
finding: Gap 7 proxy. Raters preferred GPT-3.5-written plans over entrepreneurs' own plans, so plan quality judged by raters is not a measure of what founders would test.
numbers: 10 accelerator plans (5 accepted, 5 rejected) from 309 submissions, 250 evaluators. LLM plans rated +0.14 s.d. (p<0.001), +5 points more likely to be recommended (p=0.003). Versus plans that were accepted by the accelerator, LLM version +7 points accept (p=0.003).
limits: Only 10 plans, GPT-3.5, no outcome data. Measures perceived quality, not experiments run.
agent_relevance: No field study was found that compares LLM-proposed cheap experiments with the experiments founders ran. Gap 7 stays open.

source: Csaszar, Ketkar and Kim (2024) LLM vs investor scores
finding: LLM scores of business plans correlate moderately with investor scores.
numbers: 138 plans from a startup competition. Correlation 0.52. LLM scores explain about 29% of investor score variance. KS test on distributions p=0.86.
limits: Agreement with investors is not accuracy about outcomes.
agent_relevance: Fine for screening, not for forecasting venture success (links to claim K16).

finding: Gap 7 proxy. LLM founder personas gave overlapping themes with 15 real founders, but warned that synthetic users can inflate optimism through polite lies. No predictive test.
numbers: 15 human founders interviewed (Dec 2024 to Jan 2025); 35 synthetic personas (30 founders, 5 investors). No overlap counts or accuracy reported.
limits: Qualitative; author states predictive accuracy was not tested.
agent_relevance: LLM-simulated customers for assumption tests risk false positives; require real or behavioral evidence.

source: When Two LLMs Debate, Both Think They'll Win (2025)
finding: Gap 5 proxy. When models argue a side, stated win probability rises with each round. Adversarial arguing makes models more, not less, confident. No mitigation was reported on the page read.
numbers: 60 three-round debates, 10 LLMs. Mean initial confidence 72.9% against 50% rational baseline; final round mean 83%. Both sides at 75% or more in 61.7% of debates. Self-debate rose 64.1% to 75.2%; told 50%, rose 50.0% to 57.1%.
limits: Debate between two models, not a single-agent devil's advocate or premortem. Read from the abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Naive devil's-advocate role play may inflate confidence in whichever side is argued. A separate neutral scorer is safer than a self-argued pro and con.

source: DiNCo (2025) calibrating verbalized confidence with self-generated distractors
finding: Closest measured 'consider the alternatives' step for overconfidence. Having the model generate distractor claims and compare confidence cuts calibration error versus plain verbalized confidence, at about 10 calls. It is a factual-QA method, not a premortem.
numbers: ECE TriviaQA Qwen3-8B 0.097 vs best baseline 0.149; Llama-3.2-3B 0.044 vs 0.065; Gemma-3-4B 0.121 vs 0.252; Qwen3-1.7B worse (0.177 vs 0.104). SimpleQA GPT-4.1 ECE 0.089 vs 0.263, but AUC 0.786 vs 0.800. 10 calls, about 32% more FLOPs than self-consistency; DiNCo at 10 calls beats self-consistency at 100.
limits: Factual QA and biographies only. Mixed on one small model and on AUC. Not tested on forecasts or plans.
agent_relevance: Generating competing alternatives and normalizing confidence over them is a calibrated way to implement 'what else could be true', cheaper than 100 samples.

finding: Frontier models stay overconfident on coding tasks. History-in-context plus a prompt to be more judicious reduced overconfidence for some Claude models and GPT-4.5, mostly by accepting fewer contracts. Reflection after submission raised AUROC for several Sonnet models.
numbers: Experiment 1: 1,140 BigCodeBench tasks; Experiment 2: 512 sequences of 9 contracts (+$1 or -$1); Experiment 3: 499 SWE-Bench Verified tasks, 70-tool-call budget. All models overconfident in Experiments 1 and 2. Exact point values only in figures.
limits: No premortem or devil's-advocate arm tested. Coding tasks. Numbers not in text.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for premortem. Experience-based correction (past failures in context) is the one lever with measured effect.

source: Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz and Koning (2024) Uneven impact of generative AI on entrepreneurial performance (search summaries)
finding: Search snippets only. Version difference: working paper reports low performers about 8% worse; published version nearly 10%. Mechanism is selection of generic advice (price cuts), not the questions asked. No follow-up for other advisers was found.
numbers: 640 Kenyan business owners, high performers just over 15% better, low performers 8% (working paper) or nearly 10% (published) worse.
limits: Not opened this session; relies on search summary. Gap 8 stays open: no replication with other advisers and no test of a riskiest-assumption-forcing prompt was found.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a forced-assumption prompt removes the harm; it is untested.

source: Camuffo et al. (2024) Strategic Management Journal replication, abstract page
finding: Abstract confirms four RCTs and 759 firms, more terminated ideas, and a nonlinear pivot pattern (few radical pivots rather than none or many). Full text was blocked (403 on Wiley, City, Polito, CEPR), so revenue effects and panel fragility could not be checked.
numbers: 759 firms, four RCTs. A search summary adds Milan 2017, Turin 2018, London 2019 and 11,463 data points (not verified in text).
limits: Published SMJ article (vol 45 issue 6, pp 1209-1237), not only a working paper. Revenue and pivot coefficients not read. Gap 3 stays open.
agent_relevance: Keep claim K07 for pivot and termination direction; revenue replication unverified.

source: Search for premortem or devil's advocate prompting on LLM overconfidence (2 searches)
finding: No paper was found that tests a premortem, prospective hindsight, or devil's advocate prompt on LLM calibration. Nearest are FOReCAst (poor calibration, no consistent link between accuracy and calibration), debate overconfidence (d12) and DiNCo (d13).
numbers: None. Mitchell et al. 1989 (30% more reasons) remains unverified and should not be cited.
limits: Negative search result, search snippets only. Absence is not proof.
agent_relevance: Treat premortem as an untested design choice; measure it ourselves against a no-premortem arm.

source: Search for assumption-mapping steps versus plain reasoning at equal tokens (gap 1)
finding: No benchmark was found that compares 'list assumptions, rank by risk, design one test' with plain reasoning at equal tokens. Popper (d06) and Failing to Falsify (d04) test pieces of the loop in narrow domains.
limits: Negative result from search and the sources opened; not exhaustive.
agent_relevance: This is a clean experiment for our own harness: assumption-map arm vs plain arm vs best-of-N at matched tokens.
